item.title: How we built the AssetHoard MCP server
item.dc:creator: Mark Gandolfo
item.description: AssetHoard's built-in MCP server lets Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code and Windsurf search your asset library and export into your game project. How we built it.
item.content:encoded:
You're three hours into building a level. You need a barrel. You know you own at least four barrel packs, because you bought them in three different bundle sales and one of them was "a steal". Finding them means leaving the editor, opening a file browser, and digging through folders called Downloads (2).

Meanwhile there's an AI assistant sitting in your editor that can write a state machine in eight seconds but has no idea what's on your hard drive.

AssetHoard is a local-first desktop asset manager for indie game developers and digital artists, and version 0.2.3 fixes that with a built-in MCP server. This post covers how we built it, why it's locked down the way it is, and the things we've found it genuinely useful for.

What MCP is, briefly

The Model Context Protocol is an open standard for letting AI tools call other programs. A program exposes a set of named tools with typed arguments ("search", "export", "create_bundle"), and any MCP client (Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code, Windsurf, Claude Desktop) can discover and call them.

For an asset manager that's a natural fit. AssetHoard already knows every model, texture, sprite and sound you own, what's in which bundle, what it's tagged, and what each file depends on. MCP lets your assistant ask it.

The decisions that shaped it

Built into the app, not a separate program

The obvious shortcut would have been a little standalone server that opens AssetHoard's SQLite database and reads it directly. We didn't do that, for two reasons.

First, two programs writing to one SQLite file is how you end up with a corrupted library and a very bad afternoon. Second, the app would never find out about changes. You'd ask your assistant to tag forty rocks and the open window would keep showing them untagged until you restarted.

So the server runs inside AssetHoard itself, and the app has to be open for it to answer. That turned out to be a feature: every change the assistant makes shows up in the window straight away.

Living inside the app also means you stay in charge of it from the app:

  • Turn it on and off. One switch in Settings > MCP Server. It's off until you flip it, and a plug icon sits in the toolbar whenever it's running, so you're never guessing.
  • See what changed. When an assistant exports files or edits your library, AssetHoard shows a notification in the app saying what it did, and the settings page keeps a list of recent calls.
  • Decide how much the assistant can do. Out of the box it can only search, look and export. Changing your library needs "Allow write tools" switched on, and importing files pops up a prompt you have to approve. If you'd rather keep it read-only forever, just leave the write switch off.

One rule: MCP never touches the database directly

The MCP code lives in its own module, and it isn't allowed to call app commands or SQL. Everything goes through a small internal library API that sits underneath both the UI and the MCP server.

That sounds like bureaucracy, but it's what makes the write tools trustworthy. When an assistant moves an asset into a bundle, it runs exactly the same function as when you drag it there yourself. Same validation, same audit log, same undo entry. There's no second, slightly different code path quietly drifting out of sync with the real one.

It also makes adding a tool cheap. A new tool is a typed argument struct (whose doc comments become the descriptions the model reads) and a thin method that calls the library API. The interesting logic stays in one place and gets tested once.

Rust, rmcp and streamable HTTP

AssetHoard's backend is Rust, so we used rmcp, the official Rust SDK for MCP, with its streamable HTTP transport mounted on axum. Database work runs on blocking worker threads so a big search never stalls the app's async runtime, and each call is recorded in a recent-activity list you can watch in Settings.

We picked HTTP over stdio because the server lives inside a desktop app that's already running. Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code and Windsurf all connect to a local HTTP endpoint with a header, which is a one-line setup. Claude Desktop is the odd one out: it only launches stdio servers, so for now it connects through the mcp-remote bridge.

A fixed port, on purpose

The server listens on port 47823 by default. You can change it, but AssetHoard will never pick a different one on its own if that port is busy. Auto-switching sounds helpful until every client config you've written silently stops matching. Instead, a taken port shows up as an error with a readable message, and you choose what to do.

Making it safe to leave on

A local server that can read your files and write to your library deserves some paranoia. Here's what's in place:

  • Off by default. You turn it on in Settings > MCP Server.
  • Local only. It binds to 127.0.0.1, so nothing on your network or the internet can reach it.
  • Token required. Every request needs a bearer token: 48 random hex characters, compared in constant time. Regenerating it disconnects every client.
  • Browsers are refused. Any request with an Origin header is rejected, and the Host header must be a loopback address. Browsers always send Origin; CLI and IDE clients don't. This blocks DNS rebinding, where a malicious web page tries to talk to a server on your machine, and it's what the MCP spec asks local servers to do.
  • Write tools are a second opt-in. "Allow write tools" is a separate toggle, and it's checked on every call, so switching it off takes effect immediately, even for clients that are already connected.
  • No deleting your stuff. There are no tools for deleting assets or bundles. The only deletes are for categories nothing uses and projects that are already empty.
  • Exports never overwrite. If a file already exists at the destination, it's skipped and reported.
  • Imports ask first. When an assistant wants to import a folder, AssetHoard pops up a prompt with the path, file count, size and target bundle, and flashes the window. No answer within 60 seconds counts as no. If you trust your setup, "Import without asking" turns this off.
  • Everything is undoable. Writes go on the normal undo stack with an MCP: label, like MCP: Moved 1 asset into 'Rocks', and a toast tells you what changed. Ctrl+Z (Cmd+Z on a Mac) works exactly as it does for your own edits.

A plug icon appears in the toolbar whenever the server is running, so you always know it's on.

Small things that made a big difference

Search returns text, thumbnails are separate. Search results are ids, names, types, paths and tags, which keeps them small. If the assistant wants to actually look at something, it calls get_thumbnail and gets a preview image of at most 256 pixels. That means it can check that the "mossy rock" really is mossy before suggesting it, without flooding its context with every result's picture.

Dependencies come along. Exporting a model brings its textures. Exporting a Godot .tres brings the files it references, and Unreal assets bring theirs. Exporting a whole bundle keeps its folder layout. Assets inside zip archives or .unitypackage files are pulled out first.

Clickable links. Every asset, bundle and project the server returns includes an assethoard:// link. The assistant can hand you a link, you click it, and AssetHoard jumps to that item. We added the link scheme to the app specifically for this.

Errors the model can read. An unknown id, a bundle inside a package, or write tools being switched off all come back as plain error messages rather than protocol failures, so the assistant can explain what happened or try something else.

What you can do with it

Here's what this looks like in practice. These are the kinds of things you'd type into Claude Code, Cursor or similar with AssetHoard running.

Set dressing without leaving the editor

"Find three different barrel models and a wood texture that matches, and copy them into Assets/Props."

The assistant searches your library, looks at the thumbnails of the best few, picks a set and exports them, textures included. You keep building the level. This was the main use case we designed for, and it's the one in the demo video.

Search by what it looks like, not what it's called

"Do I have any mossy stone wall textures?"

Search works the same way as AssetHoard's search bar: by name with typo tolerance, and by meaning when semantic search is turned on. Since 0.2.3 that includes embedded audio metadata too, so "glass shatter" can find SFX_0472_FINAL.wav if that's what its description says.

Narrow it down like you would in the app

"Show me Godot UI sprites from my Kenney bundle."

Results can be filtered by file type, asset class, engine, tag, category or bundle. The assistant works out the bundle id itself and filters inside it.

Drop a whole tileset into a project

"Copy my 'Dungeon Tileset' bundle into the Godot project at C:/dev/crawler."

The bundle's sub-bundles become folders in the destination, so the structure you set up in AssetHoard carries over.

Tidy up the library (write tools on)

"Make a bundle called 'Rocks' under 'Environment', move every rock model into it and tag them 'nature'."

The assistant creates the bundle, searches, moves and tags. Each step appears live in the app and is its own undo entry. If it gets carried away and moves a boulder that was actually a potato, Ctrl+Z.

A slower but satisfying variation: "Find the untagged textures in my Downloads bundle, look at each one and suggest tags." Review the suggestions, say yes, and let it apply them.

Keep track of what a game uses

"Start a project called 'Crawler' and add the dungeon tileset and the footstep sounds to it."

Projects in AssetHoard only record references. Nothing moves, and an item can belong to several projects. Once a project is set up, you can ask questions like "list everything in Crawler and tell me which assets have no licence recorded", which is a much nicer way to find out before release than after.

Onboard a new pack

"Import C:/Users/me/Downloads/kenney_platformer-pack into my Kenney bundle, then categorise the new assets by type."

AssetHoard asks you to allow the import, runs it through the normal import queue with the usual progress notification, then the assistant categorises what came in. The whole import is one undo entry.

What's next

The main gap right now is Claude Desktop needing the mcp-remote bridge. A small native shim that lets it connect directly is on the list. We'd also like to hear what you end up using the server for, because the tool list was shaped by our own workflow and yours is probably weirder.

Try it

The MCP server is in AssetHoard 0.2.3 and later. Open Settings > MCP Server, switch it on, and paste the setup command into your client. The MCP docs cover each client, and the tool reference lists every tool and its arguments. AssetHoard is free to download during the open beta, so the only thing it'll cost you is finally finding out how many barrel packs you own.

The AssetHoard Team

item.title: How to stay motivated as a solo indie developer
item.dc:creator: Mark Gandolfo
item.description: Motivation runs out on every long project. Solo indie developers who finish rely on habits, visible progress and real rest to get through the slow middle.
item.content:encoded:
Every solo dev I know has hit the same wall. The first few weeks of a project are electric. You can see the whole thing in your head, the ideas won't stop coming, and you'd happily skip meals to keep building. Then, somewhere around week six or month three, the electricity goes out. The work is still there. The excitement isn't.

This isn't a character flaw and it isn't a sign you picked the wrong project. It's the shape of every long piece of solo work. You will not feel motivated all the time, because nobody does. What you can do is build something that keeps you moving when the motivation is gone.

The short version

If you only take a few things away, take these. The rest of the post unpacks each one.

  • Stop waiting to feel motivated. Build habits that still produce something on a flat day.
  • Shrink the next task until it's almost embarrassingly small, then start there.
  • Set a daily minimum you can hit even on your worst day, and protect the streak.
  • Keep a visible record of what you've finished, on screen or on paper.
  • Beat isolation on purpose: find other devs, post devlogs, get one person to hold you to it.
  • Compare yourself to last month's you, never to someone else's finished game.
  • Treat rest, food, exercise and people as part of the schedule, not a reward you earn.

Motivation is a bad thing to depend on

Motivation is a feeling, and feelings come and go for reasons you don't control. You slept badly. The bug you spent all day on wasn't the real bug. Someone posted a screenshot of their game that made yours look like a student project. Any of those can flatten your drive for a day, and if your ability to work depends on feeling driven, you've just lost a day.

The developers who finish things have arranged their work so that a flat day still produces something. They've quietly stopped asking "do I feel like working" and started asking "what's the next small thing I said I'd do".

Shrink the task until it's stupidly small

When you can't face the work, the task in your head is almost always too big. "Build the inventory system" is not a task, it's a project, and staring at it does nothing but make you tired.

The fix is to shrink the next step until it's almost embarrassingly small. Not "build the inventory system" but "add one slot to the inventory grid". Not "do the audio pass" but "wire up the sound for the door opening". A task you can picture finishing in twenty minutes is a task you can start, and starting is the whole problem. Momentum almost always shows up once you're moving, it just refuses to show up beforehand.

On genuinely bad days, shrink it further. Open the project. Read the code you wrote yesterday. That's allowed to be the whole session. More often than not, once the file is open you'll fix one small thing, and one small thing is infinitely more than zero.

Set a daily minimum you can hit on your worst day

Pick a floor. Something so small that you'd feel silly not doing it even when you're exhausted or fed up. Fifteen minutes. One commit. One asset placed. One line of design doc.

The output barely matters. What the minimum protects is the streak. A chain of tiny days keeps the project alive in your head and stops the restart cost from piling up. If you skip a project for a fortnight, coming back costs you an afternoon just remembering where you were. If you touched it yesterday, you're already warm.

Some days you'll hit the minimum and stop, and that's fine. Plenty of days you'll hit the minimum and then keep going for two hours because you were never really tired, you were just staring at something too big. The minimum only has to get you to the desk. Most of the time, once you're there, you keep going.

Make progress visible, because your brain won't do it for you

The cruel thing about the middle of a project is that progress stops feeling like progress. The exciting, visible milestones are behind you and ahead of you, and the middle is a thousand small tasks that don't individually look like much. Left alone, your brain will happily conclude you've done nothing for a month.

So don't leave it alone. Keep a record it can't argue with. A "done" list you actually add to, a devlog you post every week whether or not anyone reads it, a folder of dated screenshots you can scroll back through. When the doubt shows up, you want evidence sitting right there. The version of your game from three months ago is the proof, and if you never captured it, the doubt wins by default.

None of this has to happen in front of a computer either. Grab a notebook and sketch the inventory system you've been putting off. Scribble down a world-building idea before it evaporates. Draw the level on graph paper. A page of notes from a walk is still a record of a day you moved the project forward, and some days it's the easiest kind to make.

This is one place a bit of tooling earns its keep. Being able to scroll back through what you've built, the sprites you've drawn, the models you've made, the packs you've assembled, is a quiet antidote to the feeling that you're standing still. Half the time you're much further along than it feels. (It's a big part of why I organise my asset library so I can actually see it.)

Isolation is the real enemy, not the work

The work is rarely what breaks people. Working entirely alone for months is what breaks people. No colleague to tell you the idea's good. Nobody to notice you shipped the thing. No standup where you say out loud what you did yesterday and quietly realise it was quite a lot.

You have to manufacture what a team gives you for free. Find a Discord of other solo devs (the AssetHoard Discord is one) and actually turn up in it. Post your devlog even to an audience of nine. Tell one friend what you're shipping this week so there's a human who'll ask how it went. Pair up with another dev and trade weekly check-ins. None of this is marketing. It keeps the work real to someone other than you. Externalising your progress to even one other person changes how the work feels, because suddenly you're not the only one who knows it exists.

If in-person is an option, take it. A monthly indie meetup or a game jam can reset your whole outlook in an afternoon, mostly by reminding you that everyone else is also stuck on something and doubting themselves too.

Stop comparing your middle to someone else's end

The screenshot that ruined your afternoon was a finished, polished, cherry-picked frame of someone else's months of unglamorous work. You compared it to your actual Tuesday, bugs and placeholder art and all. Of course you lost.

Everything you see online is a highlight. The trailer, the launch post, the "we hit a thousand wishlists" thread. You don't see the fortnight they spent fighting the same engine bug you're fighting, or the three redesigns they binned, or the week they didn't open the project at all. Comparison isn't just unkind to yourself, it's inaccurate, because you're missing most of the data.

The only honest comparison is you against you. Are you further along than last month? Then it's working.

Protect your life, not just your rest

A lot of solo devs treat rest as a reward they have to unlock by working hard enough, which means they never quite unlock it, which means they run flat out until they crash. Then they lose two weeks to burnout and call themselves lazy for it.

Rest isn't earned, it's part of the schedule. So is eating well, exercising, and spending time with friends and family. None of that is what you do once the real work is finished, it's the space that lets you recharge between sessions of the real work. Build it in on purpose. Take one full day off a week and don't touch the project. Stop at a set time most evenings. Go outside. The ideas that untangle your worst problems almost never arrive while you're grinding at the desk, they turn up in the shower, on a walk, doing the washing up. A rested brain is a faster brain, and a burned-out one ships nothing at all.

Burnout is not a badge. It's a project risk, and it's your job to manage it like any other.

What it actually takes

Staying motivated as a solo dev is mostly a matter of not needing to be motivated. You build small habits, you make your progress visible, you find a few humans to be accountable to, you rest before you're wrecked, and you keep comparing yourself only to yesterday's version of yourself.

Do that, and the flat days stop being a threat. They become just another Tuesday where you hit your minimum, close the laptop, and come back tomorrow. The people who finish games aren't superhuman. They just kept turning up through the boring middle, one small task at a time, until the finish line quietly showed up.

Keep turning up.

The AssetHoard Team

item.title: Artist spotlight: James Rommel Lobaton, Spine 2D animator
item.dc:creator: The AssetHoard Team
item.description: 2D/3D game animator James Rommel Lobaton on rigging other artists' work in Spine, his commission process, and what indie devs should know before hiring one.
item.content:encoded:
Welcome back to our Artist Spotlight series, where we chat with creators in the game dev space about their work, their process, and what they've learned along the way.

This time we're talking to James Rommel G. Lobaton, a 2D and 3D game animator from the Philippines with ten years in the industry, a Unity Asset Store shop, and a portfolio that swings happily between Dota 2, fighting games, horror icons and anime.

For readers who haven't come across your work yet, what do you do?

I'm a 2D/3D game animator, and I've been in the animation industry for ten years now. I create animation for games, and on the side I take commissions for character designs and creatures.

During the day I work at a local game dev studio in the Philippines. After work I go home and work again on freelance jobs.

We also have a Unity Asset Store shop, where my friends and I make 2D chibi assets for games. Some are PNGs, and some are bundles with animations ready to drop into a game.

How did you end up working across both 2D and 3D, and was game development always the goal?

I started late on this path. Before animation I was a delivery guy, delivering special welding rods to industrial companies. Animation is my second chance.

I studied a vocational 3D animation course, and from there I threw myself into learning everything about 3D, trying to be a one-man army. While I kept studying 3D, I was also learning Photoshop and basic 2D drawing.

Then I got the opportunity to work at a game dev studio as a 3D animator. As the project went on we ran into trouble: they couldn't integrate 3D characters into a 2D environment. That's where the switch happened. I needed to learn Spine, and that's how I became a 2D/3D animator.

My teacher in the industry was into games, so all of my practice was for games. Dota 2 inspired me a lot too. So yes, I love game dev.

Your portfolio mixes Dota 2, fighting games, horror icons and anime. What shaped your style?

I've loved comics since I was a kid. I love the sharp black lines and big buckets of black against vibrant colours. Since starting on this path, I've always practised my drawing, starting with chibi characters. The style has stayed the same: black line art and cool, vibrant colours.

Games that influenced me are Hades, Borderlands, Skullgirls and Darkest Dungeon. For artists, it's Mike Mignola, Ludo Lullabi and Todd McFarlane. They're brilliant artists, and I love how unique their work is. There's so much energy in their drawings. It keeps my fire going.

And what are you drawn to right now?

I still practise and develop my style digitally, but right now I'm also doing traditional painting and drawing on the side. I love going back to watercolour, gouache and acrylic, with some oil pastels too. It's my way of not burning out, because I'm always doing something different.

On projects like Into the Crypt you animated characters drawn by another artist. How do you approach that?

Before I take a commission, I always check whether I can do cutouts in the other artist's style. I use Spine, so I need to cut the art into parts. That's why I don't take on realistic art: it's hard for me to fill in the missing parts of the drawing.

What makes a piece of art easy or hard to rig?

The hard part is when a character is complicated, like one with lots of tentacles or heavy clothing. The cutouts take time, and the rigging needs some study or research. If a character is really complicated, I need to know how the client plans for it to move so that I can do the cutouts wisely.

Take us through a typical commission, like the Bone Dragon boss. What happens between the brief and the final files?

First, the client sends all the details about the boss monster. Then I create different silhouettes, pick the ones I like and add detail. At this stage it's all sketches.

I send those to the art director so they can choose one and ask for adjustments. Then it comes back to me to polish. When everything is signed off, I start doing the cutouts for the Spine animation. The final files are delivered in a folder at the end.

What does your toolkit look like for 2D and 3D work?

I use Photoshop and Procreate for 2D, and Maya or 3ds Max for 3D, though I'm practising Blender now.

A rough animation test: the figure is drawn frame by frame in red line, with the frame numbers pencilled in.

Why Spine for game animation?

It's a very strong piece of software for quick 2D animation. It's built for games, it keeps getting better with every update, and it's a one-time payment. Spine is probably the tool I couldn't work without. It's a big part of my commission work.

Between client work, fan art and challenges like Inktober and Swordtember, how do you keep your files organised?

Staying organised is a pain. You have to name things correctly or you'll waste time looking for your files. I keep my files on Google Drive and my PC, and I name them after the game or the customer.

My biggest pain point is not having enough space on my PC's drive.

(We may know a thing or two about that one. Here's how we keep 100,000 game assets findable.)

What do you wish indie developers knew before commissioning an animator?

Know what you want first: what type of game, what animation style, what art style. Always have references. And always communicate. The faster the reply, the better.

James's character process: silhouettes first, then colour roughs, then the final character animated.

See more of James's work, or get in touch about new projects:

  • ArtStation
  • Instagram
  • LinkedIn

This is part of our Artist Spotlight series. If you're a game asset creator and want to be featured, get in touch at mark@assethoard.com.

item.title: Top Free 2D Game Assets in 2026
item.dc:creator: The AssetHoard Team
item.description: Our running roundup of the best free 2D asset packs for game developers and creative professionals, kept up to date through 2026.
item.content:encoded:
Free 2D game assets are everywhere, but the ones you can actually ship are harder to find. Half the packs you come across are free to download and not free to use, and the licence is usually buried three clicks deep or missing entirely. This is our running roundup of the free 2D game asset sources we keep coming back to, updated through 2026 (last refreshed September 2026).

A quick word before the list: free does not mean unrestricted. Most of these allow commercial use, but the exact terms vary by site and sometimes by individual asset, so treat every link below as a starting point and confirm the licence before you put anything in a build you intend to sell.

If you'd rather skip the hunt, we keep a curated directory of free CC0 assets, filterable by type, style, and source, with every licence checked so you can grab something and get back to building.

Start with the classics

If you have never gone hunting for free assets before, start with the names every game developer already has bookmarked. These are the obvious, always-recommended ones, and they cover an enormous amount of ground on their own.

  • Kenney - thousands of assets covering 2D sprites, tiles, and UI, plus 3D and audio, all released as CC0. Public domain, no attribution, commercial use fine. If you only ever use one source, make it this one.
  • itch.io game assets - the biggest indie marketplace has a deep free section full of sprite packs, tilesets, and UI kits. Licences are set by each creator, so read the terms on the page before downloading.
  • OpenGameArt - a long-running community library of free 2D and 3D art under a mix of open licences. Quality varies, but there are gems, and the licence is always stated on the asset page.

The rest of this list covers the more specialist and less obvious sources worth knowing.

What we looked for

  • Genuinely free, not a paywalled "free" teaser for a paid pack
  • A licence you can actually read and live with, ideally allowing commercial use
  • Quality that holds up next to paid work
  • Formats you can drop straight into a 2D project (PNG sprites, SVG, tilesets)

At a glance

A quick comparison to help you filter. "Commercial" is whether you can use the assets in a paid or ad-supported game, and the licence column is a summary only, so always confirm the terms on the specific asset before you ship.

Source Best for Licence Commercial
Kenney Sprites, tiles, UI CC0 Yes
itch.io Everything Varies by creator Usually
OpenGameArt Community 2D and 3D CC0, CC BY, GPL Varies
Pixabay Stock backgrounds, textures Pixabay Licence Yes, with limits
GameDev Market Backgrounds, scene art Per asset Varies
Super Game Asset RPG and skill icons Per asset (samples) Check terms
Unlucky Studio Sprites, UI, icons Per pack Yes
SVG Repo Vector icons CC0, MIT, CC BY Varies
Game-icons.net Game and ability icons CC BY 3.0 Yes, with credit
Reiner's Tilesets Sprites, textures Site licence Yes
Clip Studio Assets Brushes, tones, props Per asset Varies
Square Assets Clean 2D sets Per item Varies
Pngtree Stock PNGs Free tier Gated to paid
GameArt2D Sprites, tilesets, GUI CC0 Yes
CraftPix Sprites, GUI, backgrounds CraftPix free licence Yes, no file resale

The picks

Pixabay 2D games

A broad stock library that can fill gaps for backgrounds, textures, and reference art. The Pixabay Content Licence is generous: no attribution required and commercial use allowed, though you cannot sell unmodified content on its own, and anything featuring recognisable brands or people is off limits for commercial work. Pixabay has also had issues with copyright and AI-generated content slipping into the library, so double-check the source of anything before you use it.

Link: Pixabay 2D games

GameDev Market free 2D backgrounds

GameDev Market is a paid marketplace with a rotating free section, and its background packs are a good source of parallax layers and scene art. Licensing is set per asset rather than site-wide, and some free downloads sit behind a Pro membership, so open the asset page and read its licence panel before you commit to using it in a project.

Link: GameDev Market free 2D backgrounds

Super Game Asset free assets

Best known for its polished RPG item and skill icons. The free section is mostly sample sets offered as a taste of the paid collections, downloaded through a free account. The art quality is high, but because these are samples, read the site's licensing FAQ so you are clear on where the free tier ends and a purchase begins.

Link: Super Game Asset free assets

Unlucky Studio free game art

A well-organised stash of 2D art covering character sprites with animation, UI kits, backgrounds, weapon packs, RPG item icons, fantasy monsters, and vehicles. The studio states its free downloads can be used commercially, though attribution expectations can differ from one pack to the next, so check the individual post you are downloading from.

Link: Unlucky Studio free game art

SVG Repo

A huge searchable library of vector icons and illustrations, useful well beyond games for menus, tools, and marketing. The catch worth knowing is that assets come under a mix of licences (CC0, MIT, CC BY, and others), and each entry is tagged individually. Filter by licence and check the one on the asset you want, because "free to download" here does not automatically mean attribution-free.

Link: SVG Repo

Game-icons.net

The first place to look for UI and ability icons. It hosts over 4,000 game icons covering weapons, creatures, buildings, status effects, and abstract symbols, all available as both SVG and PNG with colour variations bundled in. The whole collection is CC BY 3.0, so commercial use is fine as long as you credit the authors. The vector format means you can recolour and scale everything to match your HUD without quality loss.

Link: Game-icons.net

Reiner's Tilesets

A veteran resource that has been giving away game art for decades. You will find 2D sprites (animals, monsters, buildings, vehicles), a large set of 3D models, and close to 300 tiling textures for walls, ground, wood, and stone. Reiner has long offered these on generous free-to-use terms including commercial projects, but the exact conditions live on the site's licence page, so read them before shipping.

Link: Reiner's Tilesets

Clip Studio Assets

The asset marketplace built into Clip Studio Paint, full of brushes, textures, tones, 3D props, and pose references. It is the right place to look if you create your art in Clip Studio, since much of it is designed to be used inside the app. If you plan to use assets elsewhere, check the individual asset's terms, as usability outside Clip Studio Paint is not guaranteed.

Link: Clip Studio Assets

Square Assets free collection

A small game-art store with a free collection sitting alongside its paid packs. Worth a look for clean, consistent 2D sets, but because it is a storefront, the free items each carry their own terms. Read the licence on the item page before downloading.

Link: Square Assets free collection

Pngtree 2D assets

An enormous general-purpose library of PNGs and graphics with a deep 2D search. Treat it with caution: the free tier typically requires attribution and has daily download limits, full commercial rights are often gated behind a paid plan, and like any large stock site, the occasional mislabelled or AI-generated item slips through. Verify the source and licence of anything you pull from here.

Link: Pngtree 2D assets

GameArt2D freebies

A tidy set of ready-to-use 2D game art: character sprites (a platformer plumber, ninjas, zombies, a knight, and more), themed tilesets covering platformer, winter, desert, sci-fi, and graveyard, and a range of GUI packs. The free assets are released as CC0, so there are no restrictions and no attribution, and they are fine for prototyping, game jams, and commercial projects alike.

Link: GameArt2D freebies

CraftPix freebies

One of the largest free 2D libraries around, with sprites, tilesets, GUI, icons, backgrounds, and full game kits added regularly. A free account is needed to download. Commercial use is allowed with no attribution required, but you cannot redistribute or resell the raw art files, and the licence forbids using the assets to train AI or machine-learning systems.

Link: CraftPix freebies

A note on licences

This is the part that trips people up. Free does not always mean unrestricted, and the difference between "CC BY" and "free for personal use only" is the difference between a safe launch and a takedown notice. Before you ship, confirm three things for every asset: is commercial use allowed, is attribution required, and can you modify it. Write the answer down somewhere that stays attached to the file, not in a browser tab you will lose by next week.

This is exactly the problem AssetHoard is built to solve. Every asset carries its own licence field, and when you import, AssetHoard will try to detect a bundled licence file and fill it in for you, with a manual override when it gets it wrong. The terms travel with the asset instead of living in your memory, so six months from now you still know whether that icon pack needs a credit line.

Wrapping up

That is the current list. We keep this page updated as sources come and go, so bookmark it and check back. When you have pulled a few packs together, download AssetHoard to keep them organised and their licences on record before the collection gets away from you.

item.title: You bought the bundle. Now find one tree.
item.dc:creator: Mark Gandolfo
item.description: Humble, itch.io and Fanatical asset bundles are the cheapest way to build a game asset library and the fastest way to lose one. Here is how to keep yours findable.
item.content:encoded:
A bundle turns up on Humble for twelve dollars: forty asset packs, a couple of hundred thousand files between them. You buy it without thinking twice, because a single character pack at full price would cost more than the whole thing. That maths holds up. I've never met anyone who regretted the purchase.

What people regret is the Tuesday six weeks later, when they need one stylised tree for a forest scene and know for a fact they own about nine hundred of them, somewhere.

What actually lands on your drive

When the bundle unlocks you get forty or fifty zip files, named however each creator felt like naming them. LowPolyNature_v2_FINAL.zip. pack3.zip. Kenney_Assets.zip, which is 140,000 files on its own. One has a .unitypackage in it and nothing else. Another is raw .fbx and .png. A third has a Godot addon folder, a set of .uasset files, and a readme explaining which is which. Two of them are the same assets from the same artist, uploaded twice under different version numbers.

Nothing shares a structure. One creator sorts by biome, another by polygon count, a third tips everything into an Assets/ folder and leaves it there. Forty packs, forty ideas about how a library should be laid out, and none of them match yours.

Why folders don't cut it here

For your own project files, a folder structure works fine. For a bundle haul it doesn't, and the reason is simple: you can't see into a zip without opening it.

To find out whether pack3.zip has the tree you want, you unzip it and look. Do that fifty times and you've lost an afternoon. So most people open two or three, take whatever is close enough, and leave the rest sealed. The bundle becomes a folder you feel slightly guilty about every time you scroll past it.

The packs you do unzip cause the opposite problem. Now there are 200,000 loose files, your file explorer stalls trying to draw thumbnails, and searching by name only helps if you already remember what the artist called the thing. tree_04_var_b.fbx isn't much of a search term.

A better default is to index the archives without extracting them: read the manifest, pull out the previews, leave the zip where it is. The haul stays compressed on disk and still becomes searchable.

The engine problem

This is the bit that trips people up, and most advice skips it because most advice assumes you only work in Unity.

Plenty of us don't. You might prototype in Godot, take a contract in Unreal, still have a GameMaker project from last year, and get Blender files from an artist friend. So the same tree can sit in your library as a bare .fbx in one pack, wrapped in a .unitypackage in another, as a .tres resource in a Godot addon, and as a .uasset you can't open outside the editor that made it.

Four formats, one tree, and most search tools understand none of them. Unity-only tools read the .unitypackage and ignore the rest. Generic file browsers treat the four as unrelated blobs. So you end up buying assets you already own, because you had no way to tell you owned them.

What helps is a catalogue that reads the formats properly: it opens a .unitypackage, walks a Godot .tres resource graph, handles .yymps and .uasset, and files all of them as the same kind of thing. The engine that wrapped the tree stops mattering.

What "findable" actually means

Once you're a few thousand assets in, "organised" isn't really the goal any more. Findable is, and it comes down to four things.

Seeing it. A cached thumbnail, generated once. Most asset hunting is visual anyway; you rarely remember the name, but you remember what it looked like.

Describing it. Name search fails because you're searching your memory of the asset, not the artist's naming scheme. Semantic search over the previews lets you type "gnarled dead tree" and find it even when the file is called T_04b.

Narrowing it. Tags you picked, rather than the folder someone else picked. The same asset can sit under "trees", "stylised", "mobile-safe" and "that Humble bundle" at once.

Shipping it. The licence travelling with the asset, instead of sitting in a readme inside a zip you've since deleted. CC0, CC-BY with attribution, the Asset Store standard licence. It's easy to ignore until the day you ship commercially, and then it matters a great deal.

A quick pass for a new bundle

Before you open a project, try this.

  1. Download the lot into one folder. Don't unzip, don't sort.
  2. Point your catalogue at the folder and let it index, overnight if it needs to. Fifty opaque zips become a set of previews you can actually look through.
  3. Skim the results once, quickly. You're not organising, just getting a rough sense of what came in.
  4. Tag the standouts and nothing else. Twenty minutes, maybe thirty assets. The rest stay findable by search, which is enough.
  5. Flag anything with an unusual licence. It's the one step that gets expensive if you skip it.

No folder hierarchy, no naming convention, no promise to sort it properly at the weekend. A bundle is cheap and broad, and that only pays off if you can search it.

The real cost

The bundle cost twelve dollars, so it feels like it cost twelve dollars. It didn't. It also cost the twenty minutes at the start of a session spent hunting for something you own, the asset you bought a second time at full price because you'd forgotten, and the scene you built with a placeholder cube because finding the real prop was more hassle than shipping the cube.

An asset you can't find isn't doing much for you. It's just disk space.

AssetHoard is a local-first desktop asset manager built for exactly this pile. It indexes archives without unpacking them, reads Unity, Godot, Unreal and GameMaker formats as first-class citizens, generates previews, and lets you search by what things look like rather than what they were named. It runs entirely on your machine, and it's a one-time purchase, not a subscription.

The next bundle you buy is only cheap if you can find what's in it. Download AssetHoard and point it at the pile.

item.title: Unreal vs Unity: which engine fits your game?
item.dc:creator: Mark Gandolfo
item.description: Unreal vs Unity, compared for indie developers in 2026. Visual fidelity, 2D and mobile, iteration speed, pricing and royalties, plus who each engine suits.
item.content:encoded:
Where Godot vs Unity is a fight about lightness and ownership, Unreal vs Unity is a fight about ambition and scale. These are the two engines most likely to power something with a big 3D world, and they pull in noticeably different directions.

If you are still deciding whether either belongs on your list at all, the first-engine guide is the better starting point. If it's these two on the table, here is how they actually compare.

The short version

Unreal is the fidelity powerhouse, the engine studios reach for when they want photoreal lighting, vast detailed worlds, and visuals that make players ask whether they are watching a game or a film. Unity is the versatile all-rounder, lighter to run, faster to iterate in, and dominant on mobile and in 2D.

Pick Unreal for cutting-edge 3D and cinematic ambition. Pick Unity for mobile, 2D, rapid iteration, and a gentler road in. Now the detail.

Visual fidelity

This is Unreal's headline act. Its modern rendering feature set, including its dynamic global illumination and virtualised geometry systems, lets small teams produce visuals that used to require a large studio. Out of the box, for high-end 3D, it looks stunning.

Unity is very capable in 3D and its render pipelines have matured a great deal, but matching Unreal's top-end fidelity takes more manual effort. For photoreal or graphically ambitious work, Unreal starts you closer to the finish line.

Edge: Unreal.

Iteration speed and footprint

Unity is lighter. It installs smaller, opens faster, and its edit-play loop tends to feel snappier, which matters enormously when you are testing an idea for the hundredth time in an afternoon. That responsiveness is a real, daily productivity advantage, especially on modest hardware.

Unreal is a large engine with a heavier footprint, and its power comes with weight. On a capable machine it's fine; on an older laptop it can feel sluggish.

Edge: Unity.

Scripting

Unreal offers two routes: Blueprints, a powerful visual scripting system you can build entire games in without writing code, and C++ for performance-critical or lower-level work. Blueprints are a real strength and lower the barrier for non-programmers, though C++ is a demanding language once you drop into it.

Unity uses C#, which sits in a comfortable middle ground: more approachable than C++, more transferable than a visual system, and backed by a huge body of learning material. For most solo developers, C# is the more forgiving day-to-day language.

Edge: Unity for approachability, Unreal for the visual-scripting on-ramp and raw ceiling. Depends on how you like to work.

2D and mobile

Unity is the clear choice here. It has mature 2D packages, the deepest mobile toolchain of any major engine, and by far the widest third-party support for the ads, analytics and monetisation that mobile games live on.

Unreal can do 2D and mobile, but it is swimming against its own current. Its whole design centre of gravity is high-fidelity 3D, and smaller or mobile projects usually ship leaner in Unity.

Edge: Unity, decisively.

Ecosystem and assets

Both have substantial marketplaces and large communities. Unity's Asset Store is broader and especially strong for 2D, mobile and mid-scale 3D. Unreal's marketplace skews toward high-end 3D content, and Epic has a history of giving away large quantities of professional assets to Unreal developers.

Call this one close, weighted by what you are making: Unity for breadth, Unreal for high-fidelity 3D content.

Edge: Draw, project-dependent.

Pricing and royalties

The models differ in shape. Unreal is free to use and takes a royalty on gross game revenue above a threshold. Unity is free on its Personal tier and moves to paid subscriptions above revenue and funding limits.

Neither model is strictly cheaper; it depends on your revenue profile. And both companies have adjusted terms in recent years, so treat any specific figure you read, including here, as a prompt to check the current terms yourself before you commit.

Edge: Depends on your numbers. Read the current terms.

So which one?

  • Choose Unreal if: you are building ambitious 3D, you want the best-looking visuals with the least manual effort, you like Blueprints, or you are aiming at the kind of fidelity studios ship.
  • Choose Unity if: you are targeting mobile, you are doing 2D, you want faster iteration on lighter hardware, or you want a gentler entry into 3D.

For a first project, be honest about scope. Unreal's ceiling is glorious, but a small game rarely needs it, and the weight can slow you down more than the fidelity helps. Many developers are better served starting lighter and reaching for Unreal when a project truly demands it.

What both engines have in common

Whichever way you lean, the project will fill up with assets: models, textures, materials, audio, the professional packs both marketplaces hand out. That library is the part of your work that outlives the engine decision, because art and audio are just files while your Blueprints and C# are not.

AssetHoard is a local-first asset manager that keeps that library previewable and organised in one place, sitting beside whichever engine you choose. It handles the models, materials and textures these 3D-heavy workflows generate, and reads native project formats from engines like Unity, so your collection stays tidy no matter which tool you build in.

More in this series: Godot vs Unity and GameMaker vs Godot.

item.title: GameMaker vs Godot: the best engine for 2D?
item.dc:creator: Mark Gandolfo
item.description: GameMaker vs Godot, compared for 2D game development in 2026. Licensing, scripting, workflow, 3D and track record, plus which 2D engine you should pick.
item.content:encoded:
The other comparisons in this series are 3D heavyweight bouts. This one is different. GameMaker and Godot are both superb 2D engines, and choosing between them is less about raw power and more about philosophy: pure specialism versus free-and-flexible.

If you are not yet sure a 2D-focused engine is what you want, the first-engine guide zooms out. If you have narrowed it to these two, let's settle it.

The short version

GameMaker has spent decades doing one thing extremely well: 2D games. Its track record is absurd for its size, with Undertale, Hyper Light Drifter, Katana ZERO, Nuclear Throne and Hotline Miami all built in it. Godot is the free, open-source all-rounder with a first-class 2D pipeline that also happens to do 3D.

Pick GameMaker for focused 2D with the smoothest no-code-to-code ramp. Pick Godot for a free, open tool that won't box you into 2D forever. Now the detail.

Licensing and cost

Godot is free and open source under the MIT licence. No tiers, no fees, no revenue share, no catch. You own it outright.

GameMaker offers a free tier to learn and build with, and paid options for commercial release and console export. Its pricing model has shifted more than once over the years, moving between subscription and other structures, so check the current terms before you plan a commercial launch.

Edge: Godot for simplicity and permanence.

2D workflow

This is the heart of the matchup, and it's a close one.

GameMaker's entire being is 2D. Its room editor, sprite tools and 2D-specific conveniences are refined by decades of focus, and the result is a workflow that just feels made for the job. For a lot of 2D developers, that specialism is exactly the appeal.

Godot's 2D is also first-class, built on a dedicated 2D renderer and node system rather than a 3D engine wearing a flat hat. It is flexible, clean, and extremely capable. There is no 2D game GameMaker can make that Godot cannot.

Edge: Too close to call. GameMaker for refined 2D-specific polish, Godot for flexible 2D power.

Scripting

GameMaker gives you a drag-and-drop action system and its own language, GML. The pairing is one of the best beginner ramps anywhere: build logic visually to get moving, then graduate into GML when you want more control, all without switching tools.

Godot uses GDScript, a game-focused language that reads almost like plain English and is tightly woven into the engine. It skips the visual layer but is itself a very gentle first language, and Godot also supports C#.

Edge: GameMaker for the visual-to-code ramp, Godot for a clean scripting-first experience. Your preference decides it.

3D

Not really a contest, because they are aimed at different things. GameMaker is 2D by design; it has some limited 3D capability, but nobody chooses it to make a 3D game.

Godot is a full 3D engine as well, and its 3D took a major leap in the 4.x releases. If there is any chance your ambitions drift into three dimensions, Godot means you will not have to change tools to follow them.

Edge: Godot, if 3D is ever on your horizon.

Track record and community

GameMaker's hall of fame is remarkable, and it is proof that a focused 2D tool can produce genre-defining hits in the hands of small teams. Its community and learning resources are mature and 2D-centric.

Godot's community is large, fast-growing and famously welcoming, its documentation is strong, and being open source it has an unusually engaged contributor base. Both are well supported; they simply attract slightly different crowds.

Edge: Draw.

So which one?

  • Choose GameMaker if: you are certain you want 2D, you like the idea of starting with visual actions and easing into code, or you want a tool with a proven hit-making pedigree in your exact genre.
  • Choose Godot if: you want a free and open toolchain, you might one day want 3D, or you prefer a clean scripting-first workflow with no licensing tiers to track.

You can't go far wrong with either. Both are beginner-friendly, both ship real commercial games, and both respect a solo developer's time. If you want to hedge toward flexibility, lean Godot. If you want to commit fully to 2D craft, lean GameMaker.

The library outlives the engine

Whichever you choose, you will gather a pile of assets: sprites, tilesets, sound effects, fonts, the packs you download and mean to use one day. That collection is the part of your work that survives any future engine change, because your art and audio are just files while your GML or GDScript is not.

AssetHoard keeps that library previewable, searchable and organised in one place, sitting beside whichever engine you pick. It reads native project formats from both GameMaker and Godot, previewing sprites, tilesets, sounds and fonts straight from your projects, so the same tidy library follows you whichever way this decision goes.

The rest of the series: Godot vs Unity and Unreal vs Unity.

item.title: Godot vs Unity: which should you actually pick?
item.dc:creator: Mark Gandolfo
item.description: Godot vs Unity, compared for indie developers in 2026. Licensing, 2D and 3D, scripting, the asset ecosystem and mobile, plus who each engine is really for.
item.content:encoded:
This is the matchup that launches a thousand forum threads, and most of them generate more heat than light. So let's do it properly: no tribalism, no "Unity bad" or "Godot cope", just a clear look at where each engine actually earns its place.

If you haven't yet decided whether you even want these two on the shortlist, start with the broader guide to picking a first engine. If Godot and Unity are already your two finalists, read on.

The short version

Godot is the lightweight, free, open-source challenger that has spent the last few years turning from "promising" into "actually good". Unity is the established heavyweight with the biggest ecosystem in the business and a decade of industry adoption behind it.

Pick Godot if you value owning your tools, you want the simplest 2D workflow, or you want the friendliest possible on-ramp. Pick Unity if you need its enormous asset and tutorial ecosystem, you are building anything ambitious in 3D, you are targeting mobile at scale, or you want skills for a studio job. Now the detail.

Licensing and cost

This is the cleanest difference, so we'll get it out of the way first.

Godot is free and open source under the MIT licence. There is no revenue share, no per-seat fee, no runtime charge, and no threshold at which it starts costing you money. You own your copy of the engine outright, source included.

Unity has a free Personal tier for developers under a revenue and funding threshold, and paid subscription tiers above it. The technology is excellent, but it is worth remembering that Unity spent 2023 announcing a per-install runtime fee that it later walked back after significant backlash. The fee is gone, but the episode is a fair reminder that a company-owned engine can change its terms in ways an open-source one cannot.

Edge: Godot, comfortably, if predictable licensing matters to you.

2D

Godot's 2D is not a 3D engine with a flat camera bolted on. It has a dedicated 2D renderer and node system, pixel-perfect tooling, and a workflow that feels purpose-built, so you can be productive on a straightforward 2D game very quickly.

Unity's 2D is stronger than its old reputation suggests. It has a mature 2D toolset, a real 2D lighting system with normal maps and shadows, and it can bring lit 3D meshes into a 2D scene for depth and dynamic lighting that flat sprites cannot easily fake. That opens up looks Godot makes you work harder for.

Edge: Narrow, and it depends on the game. Godot for the simplest, most direct 2D workflow; Unity if you want advanced 2D lighting or to blend 2D and 3D. You make a call on what you're after.

3D

Unity wins 3D outright, and it's not close. It has built-in terrain sculpting, mature mesh handling and in-editor modelling with ProBuilder, a deep animation stack with Timeline and Cinemachine for cinematics, face and motion capture through Live Capture, and high-fidelity rendering with HDRP. On top of all that sits the largest library of ready-made 3D assets and tutorials of any engine. For anything ambitious in three dimensions, that toolset is a real head start.

Godot's 3D took a big step forward in the 4.x releases, with a rebuilt renderer, global illumination and better tooling, and it can comfortably ship a commercial 3D game, especially a stylised or smaller-scope one. But the depth is not there yet: several of those Unity systems are plugins, manual work, or simply absent in Godot.

Edge: Unity, decisively.

Lighting, post-processing and shaders

If visual polish matters to you, this is worth a closer look, and it mostly favours Unity.

On lighting and post-processing Unity is well ahead, especially through its High Definition Render Pipeline. You get volumetric lighting and fog, screen-space reflections, ray-traced options, and a Volume-based post-processing stack (bloom, colour grading, depth of field, motion blur, ambient occlusion and more) that artists can tune without touching code. Godot 4 is no slouch, with real-time global illumination through SDFGI, baked lightmaps, volumetric fog, glow and tonemapping in its Environment settings, but the range of effects and the polish of the controls do not match Unity's.

Shaders are the closer contest. Both engines let you hand-write shaders, and both ship a visual, node-based shader editor, so the core capability is comparable. Godot's shading language is clean and well documented, and plenty of people prefer it. Unity pulls ahead on the maturity of its Shader Graph and, again, the sheer volume of ready-made shaders and effects on the Asset Store.

Edge: Unity for lighting and post-processing, clearly. Shaders are closer to a draw, with Unity ahead on tooling and the asset library.

Scripting

Godot's built-in language, GDScript, is designed for game development and reads almost like plain English. It's a forgiving first language, and its tight integration with the engine makes iteration fast. You can also use C# in Godot if you prefer, with one notable catch: C# projects cannot export to the web yet, whereas GDScript can.

Unity uses C#, a mainstream, general-purpose language that looks good on a CV and transfers directly to other software work. It is more verbose than GDScript and has a slightly steeper learning curve, but the payoff is broader applicability.

Edge: Godot for approachability, Unity for transferable career skills. Call it a draw that depends on your goals.

Editor extensibility

Both engines let you script the editor itself, not just the game, and this is one of Unity's quieter strengths. Its editor scripting API is deep: you can build custom windows, inspectors, property drawers and full in-editor tools, with two UI frameworks to build them in, the older IMGUI and the newer UI Toolkit. The Asset Store is then full of editor extensions built exactly this way, so a lot of the tooling you might want already exists off the shelf.

Godot has a proper plugin system too, and it is often underrated. Scripts marked with @tool run inside the editor, and EditorPlugin lets you add custom docks, bottom panels, inspectors and gizmos. Because the whole editor is open source, you can even fork and recompile it, which is a kind of editability Unity does not offer at all. What Godot lacks is the sheer API surface and the marketplace of ready-made editor tools that Unity has spent a decade building.

Edge: Unity, for the depth of its editor API and the ecosystem of existing extensions. Godot's plugin system is capable and its open editor is uniquely moddable, but the tooling ecosystem is far smaller.

The ecosystem

Here Unity wins decisively, and it is the single strongest reason to choose it. The Unity Asset Store is deep and battle-tested, almost any "how do I do X" already has a YouTube answer, and studios list Unity by name in job adverts more than any other engine. When you hit a wall, the odds that someone has already documented the way through it are simply higher.

Godot's community is smaller but famously friendly, its documentation is solid, and its asset library grows every year. For a beginner it rarely bites, but on a complex project the ecosystem gap is real.

Edge: Unity.

Mobile

Both engines export to iOS and Android. Unity has the deeper mobile story: more mature build tooling, better-trodden performance-optimisation paths, and far more third-party support for ads, analytics and monetisation. If mobile at commercial scale is your target, Unity is the safer bet today.

Edge: Unity.

So which one?

  • Choose Godot if: you want the simplest 2D workflow, you are learning to code, you want a small fast tool, or you want a toolchain nobody can change the price of.
  • Choose Unity if: you need its ecosystem, you are targeting mobile seriously, you want job-transferable C# skills, or you are building an ambitious 3D project and want the most assets and tutorials to lean on.

And if you truly can't decide, download Godot this afternoon. It costs nothing, installs in seconds, and you'll learn more from an hour of building than from a week of comparison tables like this one.

The part that survives whichever you pick

Whichever engine wins your shortlist, one thing is identical in both: you will accumulate assets. Sprites, models, audio, fonts, texture packs, the free bundles you grab and mean to use later. That pile grows fast, and it is the one part of your project that carries across unchanged if you ever switch engines, because assets are just files while code is not.

AssetHoard is a local-first asset manager that sits beside either engine and keeps that library previewable, searchable and organised in one place. It reads native project formats from both Godot and Unity, so the same library works no matter which side of this debate you land on, or if you change your mind later.

Next in the series: Unreal vs Unity and GameMaker vs Godot.

Mark

item.title: What game engine should I start with?
item.dc:creator: Mark Gandolfo
item.description: The best game engine for beginners in 2026, explained simply. How to choose between Godot, Unity, Unreal, GameMaker and the no-code tools for your first game.
item.content:encoded:
It is the first question almost everyone asks, and it arrives loaded with more anxiety than it deserves. Choosing a game engine feels like choosing a tattoo. Permanent, public, and destined to be judged by strangers on the internet.

But it's not a tattoo. It's a pair of boots. You want ones that fit the terrain you're walking, they'll wear in over time, and if you truly hate them you can swap them for another pair without starting your life over. Every engine below has shipped games you've heard of. None of them will stop you making something good.

So instead of asking "which engine is best", ask three smaller questions that actually have answers: what am I making, where will it run, and how do I like to work. Everything else follows from those.

The three questions that matter

What am I making? A cosy 2D farming game and a first-person 3D horror game pull toward very different tools. 2D and 3D are the first fork in the road, and picking the engine built for your dimension will save you months of fighting the grain.

Where will it run? A game aimed at phones, consoles or the browser leans on very different tooling from a desktop-only one. If you already know you want to ship to mobile or the web, weight that heavily, because export support and performance on your target platform vary a lot from one engine to the next.

How do I like to work? Some people are happy in a code editor and want a real scripting language from day one. Some people think in flowcharts and want to wire up logic visually. Some people want to write as little code as humanly possible and just ship. There's no wrong answer here. It's about matching how you think to what the tool asks of you.

Hold those three answers in your head as you read the rundown below.

The engines, one by one

Godot

The one I recommend to most people starting out. Godot is free and open source, with no account, no revenue share, no runtime fee, no strings. It's a small download, it opens in seconds, and its scene-and-node model is one of the cleanest mental models in the business.

Its 2D support is first-class rather than an afterthought bolted onto a 3D engine, and its 3D has come on enormously in the 4.x releases. GDScript, its built-in language, reads almost like plain English and is a kind first programming language. You can also use C# if you want something more career-transferable.

The trade-off is ecosystem size. There are fewer paid plugins, fewer ready-made asset packs, and a smaller (though very friendly) tutorial pile than Unity has. For a beginner, that gap rarely bites. If you are weighing the two head to head, my Godot vs Unity comparison goes deeper.

Best for: 2D games, first-time coders, anyone who values owning their tools outright

GameMaker

If your first game is 2D and you want to ship it quickly, GameMaker is a superb choice, and its track record embarrasses engines ten times its size. Undertale, Hyper Light Drifter, Katana ZERO, Nuclear Throne and Hotline Miami all came out of it.

It is built entirely around 2D, which is its whole strength. You can start with drag-and-drop actions and graduate to GML, its scripting language, when you are ready for more control. That gentle ramp from no-code to real-code is exactly what a lot of beginners need.

The catch is that it is 2D only, so the day you want to make a 3D game you will be reaching for something else. For the 2D-versus-2D call against Godot, see GameMaker vs Godot.

Best for: 2D-only projects, fast iteration, a smooth path from visual logic into code

Unity

The default of the last decade, and still an enormous, capable engine. Unity uses C#, a proper mainstream language that looks good on a CV, and it has the largest third-party ecosystem of the lot. If a specific asset pack, tutorial series or plugin exists for exactly your game, there is a strong chance it exists for Unity first.

That ecosystem is the real reason to pick it. The Asset Store is deep, the answer to almost any "how do I" is already on YouTube, and studio job listings ask for it by name more than any other engine.

Two caveats. It's heavier and more complex to get started with than Godot or GameMaker, so the beginner on-ramp is a little steeper. And Unity spent 2023 torching a lot of goodwill with a since-reversed runtime-fee announcement, which is worth knowing about even though the policy itself is gone. The tech is still excellent; just go in with clear eyes.

Best for: 3D and 2D alike, building job-ready skills, leaning on a huge asset and tutorial ecosystem

Unreal Engine

Unreal is the powerhouse. If you are chasing high-fidelity 3D, photoreal lighting, or the kind of visuals that make people ask "that is a game?", this is the tool the biggest studios reach for, and it is free until you are earning serious money.

Its Blueprints visual scripting system is powerful, so you can build a surprising amount without writing C++. But Unreal is a large, heavy, professional-grade engine all the same. For a solo beginner making their first small game, it's often more engine than the project needs, and the learning curve is the steepest here. It also assumes a fairly modern machine, so on an older or low-spec laptop it will feel sluggish in a way Godot and Unity will not. If you are choosing between the two big 3D engines, my Unreal vs Unity breakdown weighs them up.

Best for: ambitious 3D, cutting-edge visuals, developers who know they want the AAA toolset

The no-code tools: Construct and GDevelop

If the word "scripting" makes you want to close the tab, start here. Construct and GDevelop let you build complete, shippable games out of visual event sheets, no traditional programming required. They run in the browser, they are quick to learn, and they are brilliant for getting a real, playable thing in front of people fast.

You will eventually hit a ceiling that code-based engines do not have, but "eventually" might be several finished games away, and finishing games is the whole point.

Best for: absolute beginners, non-programmers, rapid prototyping, small 2D projects

A quick cheat sheet

  • I want 2D and I am new to code: Godot or GameMaker.
  • I want 2D and I do not want to code at all: GDevelop or Construct.
  • I want 3D and I am new: Godot first, Unity if you need its ecosystem.
  • I want the most job-transferable skills: Unity (C#).
  • I want the best-looking 3D and I am ambitious: Unreal.
  • I can't decide: Godot. Download it today, you'll lose nothing.

The thing nobody wants to hear

The engine isn't what's standing between you and a finished game. Scope is.

The most common failure in game development has nothing to do with the engine. It's starting a sprawling dream project, burning out on it, and quietly shelving it six weeks later with nothing to show. The engine you agonised over for a week barely registers next to that.

So whatever you pick, make something tiny first. A game that fits in one screen. Something you can finish in a weekend and then actually release, warts and all. You will learn more from shipping one embarrassing little game than from a month of comparison videos, and you will find out whether the boots fit by walking in them, not by reading the box.

Whatever you pick, your assets will pile up

The moment you start, you begin collecting stuff. Sprite packs, sound effects, models, fonts, that free tileset bundle you grabbed at 2am and will absolutely use one day. It happens in every engine, and it happens fast.

That collection is the one thing that outlives your engine choice. Your art, audio and models are just files, and they carry across unchanged if you ever switch. The code does not, but the assets do. Which is exactly why it pays to keep them organised and engine-agnostic from the very beginning, rather than as a folder called assets_final_v3_USE_THIS_ONE.

That is the job AssetHoard does. It sits beside whichever engine you land on, previewing and organising your whole library in one place, and it reads native project formats from Godot, Unity and GameMaker so the same library follows you wherever you go.

Pick an engine. Make something small. Keep your assets tidy. The rest is just practice.

Mark
